subject: mathematics
question_text: Find all values of x ≠ 0 in (−π, π) satisfying 8^(1 + cos x + cos²x + … ∞) = 4³.

mark_split.label: List the values in the interval

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.108, chapter 9 TRIGONOMETRIC EQUATIONS, Short Answer question 3. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 shape puts a full mark on the SERIES, because the trigonometry in this question is easy and the marks are really lost at the sum: a student who writes 1/(1 − cos x) without stating |cos x| < 1 has assumed the series converges. The convergence condition is written into the LINES the student reads, not parked here — it is what excludes x = 0 and it is the reason the stem says x ≠ 0. Inside (−π, π) the only value with |cos x| = 1 is x = 0 (x = ±π are not in the open interval), so x = 0 is the only exclusion, and the two answers x = ±π/3 both have |cos x| = 1/2 < 1. Nothing is squared and no denominator is cleared after that point, so no extraneous root can enter. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, under the 2026-27 pattern; Trigonometric Equations supplies one of them. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — name each move in order, and say what condition the infinite series needs before it can be summed.

steps.label: Sum the infinite series
steps.margin_note: First mark. The exponent is a geometric series with first term 1 and common ratio cos x. It has a sum only when |cos x| < 1, and inside (−π, π) that rules out x = 0 — which is why the question excludes it.
steps.memory_tip: First term 1, common ratio cos x, so the sum is 1/(1 − cos x) — but only while |cos x| < 1.

geometric series with first term a = 1 and
It has a sum only if |cos x| < 1.
In (−π, π) that rules out x = 0 alone, and
∴ Sum S = a/(1 − r) = 1/(1 − cos x)

recall.must_convey: That the exponent is a geometric series with ratio cos x summing to 1/(1 − cos x), valid only when |cos x| < 1.

steps.why: An infinite geometric series has a sum only when its common ratio is smaller than 1 in size. Stating that condition is what makes the rest of the working legal.
common_mistakes: Writing the sum as 1/(1 + cos x).
Summing the series without stating |cos x| < 1.
Using the finite-series formula a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r).

steps.label: Match the powers
steps.margin_note: Second mark. 4³ is 64 and 8² is also 64, so both sides can be written to the base 8. Equal bases mean equal powers.
steps.memory_tip: 4³ = 64 = 8², so put both sides to base 8. Equal bases, equal powers.

recall.must_convey: That 4³ = 64 = 8², so the exponents match and S = 2.
accept: four cubed is sixty four which is eight squared so the power S equals two

equate the indices after matching the base

steps.why: Two powers of the same base are equal only when the exponents are equal. Writing 4³ as 8² is the one move that turns an index equation into an ordinary one.
common_mistakes: Equating the powers while the bases are still 8 and 4.

steps.label: Solve for cos x
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Put the sum equal to 2 and solve the small fraction equation. Cross-multiplying is safe here because 1 − cos x is not zero.
steps.memory_tip: 1/(1 − cos x) = 2 means 1 − cos x = 1/2, so cos x = 1/2.

recall.must_convey: That 1/(1 − cos x) = 2 gives cos x = 1/2.

steps.why: The index work and the series sum are both finished, and only a single ordinary trigonometric equation is left. From here it is the standard cosine work.

steps.label: List the values in the interval
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The interval is given, so the general solution is working and the finite list is the answer. Only n = 0 lands inside (−π, π), and both values keep |cos x| < 1.
steps.memory_tip: An interval is given, so the answer is the LIST, not the general solution. Only n = 0 fits inside (−π, π).

steps.why: When an interval is given, the general solution is only working — the answer is the finite list inside it. Both values must also keep the series summable, so the condition from step 1 is checked once more.
common_mistakes: Leaving x = 2nπ ± π/3 as the final answer.
Giving only x = π/3 and dropping the negative value.
Including x = 5π/3, which is outside (−π, π).
